To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there were 117 million EDs in the United States in 2007; 25 percent of ED visits were covered by either Medicaid or the State children's Health Insurance Program; 21 percent of ED visits by persons under 15 years of ages were to pediatric ED's; there were 121 EDs for asthma per 1,000 persons under 5 years old; 2 percent of ED visits resulted in admission for observation; and 62 percent of emergency departments used electronic medical records.
there were 117 million emergency department (ED), or urgent care visits in 2008, and 25 percent were covered by Medicaid and SCHIP.
there were about 115 million ED visits in 2005, 25% of which were covered by Medicaid and 21% by Medicare.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods and models that are useful in the analysis of health and medical data and in the development of new statistical methods.
the development of a new approach to the study of the evolution of the universe.

the following topics: • The development of methods to analyze the data from the NHAMCS and other national health care surveys, and • The use of the data to study the epidemiology of diseases and injuries, to evaluate medical care and to assess the health care needs and utilization of the population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 117 million visits to emergency department in 2007 in the United States was a record high and the leading injury related cause for emergency department visits was unintentional fall.
the data presented in this report provide a useful snapshot of the ED in the United States and are a valuable tool for health policy makers, researchers, and health care providers.

the National Hospital Ambulatory Care Survey (NHAMCS) is a national probability sample survey of visits to hospital outpatient departments and emergency rooms, conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the National Hospital Ambulatory Care Survey is an excellent source of data for the study of emergency medicine.
we have a lot of data on EDs, and it would be useful for us to have a way to make that data more accessible and more understandable.
we have a system that is in need of reform, and we need to work together with our colleagues to make the changes that need to be made.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of ED visits are not emergencies.
the ED is the most accessible point of medical care.
EDs are a major source of care for the nation's population, especially children and the elderly.
